newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian PM pledges probe into Somali torture claim.
newsitem.headline: Italian PM pledges probe into Somali torture claim.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Friday demanded an urgent inquiry into allegations that Italian soldiers tortured Somalis during a peace-keeping mission to the east African country in 1993.
The weekly news magazine Panorama published photographs earlier on Friday taken by a member of an elite Italian parachute regiment, showing soldiers abusing Somali prisoners.

One of the pictures shows an officer preparing to apply electrodes to the hands and testicles of a young Somali man, lying naked and prostrate on the ground. Another soldier is seen standing on his wrist to keep him down.

"Italy is not a country which will tolerate torture and acts of this kind," Prodi told reporters while on an official visit to China. "It is clear that we must investigate this in the most scrupulous fashion and take the most severe steps."
The defence ministry also vowed to take tough action against soldiers found guilty of torture.
"It is clear that if these accusations are founded, there can be no lenience," Massimo Brutti, undersecretary at the defence ministry, told state television.
"Those responsible will be rapidly identified, because such a shadow should not hang over the armed forces," he added.

The photographs were sold to Panorama by Michele Patruno, who served as a conscript with the Folgore regiment when it went to Somalia in 1993. Patruno said he believed some of the prisoners died after being tortured.
"I never saw this myself but other soldiers who stayed in the camps told me," he told Panorama in an interview. "They died because they were already physically worn out."
It is the second time this year that soldiers involved in the ill-fated peacekeeping mission have been accused of mistreating Somalis.

Belgian's military court opened an inquiry in April after a newspaper published pictures of its soldiers holding a Somali youth over a fire and forcing others to eat worms and drink heavily salted water.
Italy carried out investigations in 1993 into the conduct of its own troops, but no charges were brought.

Patruno said Italian peacekeepers used to arrest Somalis who were caught carrying weapons. The prisoners were tortured, under the supervision of officers, to make them reveal the presence of armed groups or arms caches, he added.
At first they were denied food and water. If they refused to talk, they had the soles of their feet burnt and were electrocuted. Others were hurled against razor-wire, he said.
Panorama also published photographs of tortoises crushed by soldiers driving heavy trucks over them as part of bets on how long the animals' shells could withstand the pressure.
Italy, a former colonial power in Somalia, sent troops to the war-torn African state in 1993 as part of a 20-nation U.N. humanitarian mission, led by the United States.
The operation was designed to help distribute food around the country but soon disintegrated into a military campaign against fugitive warlord Mohamed Farah Aideed.
Three Italian peacekeepers were killed in an ambush in July, 1993. Patruno left Somalia before the ambush and said he took the pictures during his tour of duty between February and May.
He quit the army in June 1993 and is now a salesman. His photographs came to light after a journalist overheard him talking about the Somalia operation earlier this year.
Italy's latest military peacekeeping mission is in Albania, where it is leading a multi-national security force.
